Topic: Does a democratic majority's vote to expand its own power over the economy deserve any more deference than a dictator's decree, when both equally override the rule of law that protects the individual?
Machiavelli — Judgement:
A majority is merely a numerous prince, and I have never held that number confers virtue where force once did — the many can be as violent to the few as any tyrant, only they call their appetite "law."

The rule of law exists not to flatter procedure but to bind power against its own hunger; a vote that dissolves those bonds has not legitimized conquest, it has merely multiplied the conquerors. I wrote that men forget the death of a father sooner than the loss of patrimony — a democracy that seizes property by decree teaches the same lesson in different dress, and will reap the same resentment, however clean its ballot. The occupied do not feel their chains less because half their neighbors helped forge them.

Neither the one nor the many earns obedience by title alone; both must be judged solely by whether they preserve the order that lets men keep what is theirs.

*A crowd's decree and a prince's edict weigh the same on the scale of the man they dispossess.*
Thomas Paine — Judgement: A government of our own is our natural right; but a government that grants itself new dominion over the fruits of my labor is a government that has forgotten why it was hired. Society did not create the individual's rights and cannot vote them away by majority — a mob of a million is still a mob when it tramples the one, and the arithmetic of the ballot box does not transmute plunder into justice. The difference between a king and a majority that exceeds its commission is merely the number of hands on the whip; both claim a power never delegated to them, and both must answer to the same test — did the people, as individuals, consent to this specific chain? A vote that enlarges power beyond what free men could rationally have granted each other is no more legitimate than George's decrees, and deserves no more obedience. *Government is a trust, not a treasury to be looted by whichever hand holds the majority.*
Hobbes — Judgement:
The multitude's roaring "Aye" is still one Voice once they have covenanted to be reckoned as one Body — but that unity does not license the Body to tear up the very covenant that made it a Body rather than a mob. A vote to expand power over the economy is Sovereign action, legitimate in origin, since the Sovereign's office is to judge what Peace and Common Defence require, and property itself is a creature of the Commonwealth's laws, not a wall against them. But the Sovereign's warrant is functional, not sacred: it is bounded not by the individual's fictitious "rights" against it, but by the single end for which men quit the state of Nature — to escape mutual slaughter and want. A decree, democratic or tyrannical, that governs toward that end is Law; one that merely licenses faction to plunder faction while calling itself Law is Sedition dressed in ceremony. The people's numbers grant the Sovereign authority to rule the economy; they grant it no more right than a dictator to rule it so badly that Peace itself unravels.

*Number confers the right to command, not the right to command foolishly — a Leviathan that feeds on its own limbs starves by any name.*
Keynes — Judgement:
The distinction the questioner draws is a false one, and I have never accepted it. Rule of law is not a fixed inheritance handed down from some prior age of reason; it is itself a social contrivance we revise as our understanding of the economic problem deepens — and a majority acting through settled constitutional procedure to change that contrivance is doing something categorically different from a dictator's seizure, precisely because it remains answerable, reversible, and bound by the next election. The dictator's decree admits no appeal; the majority's does, by design. What matters is not whether power over the economy expands but whether it remains recallable — that is the whole of political liberty worth having, and economic laissez-faire was never part of the bargain.

A democratic majority amending its own economic powers through law is self-government correcting itself; a dictator's decree is self-government abolished.

*The rule of law was made by man to serve him, not a church to which he owes obedience regardless of the congregation's vote.*
Wollstonecraft — Judgement:
A vote to expand power is still a claim of authority, and I have always asked by what right authority binds a mind that did not consent to its particular exercise. Numbers alone confer no reason; a majority that legislates away the rights of individuals commits the same offence as the tyrant who does so by decree, for both act by will where they ought to act by reason and justice, and both treat persons as means to an aggregate end rather than beings owed an account. My own quarrel was never with government as such but with unreasoned power — the husband's or the monarch's — and a parliament that seizes the economy without regard for the individual's claim to property and liberty merely replaces one unreasoned master with five hundred. Numbers do not manufacture reason; they merely multiply the wills that must still answer to it. The dictator errs alone; the majority errs in chorus, but an error sung by many voices is not thereby made true.

*A thousand wills unchecked by reason are tyranny with better arithmetic.*
